summary: Defines SNMP management objects for devices that implement FDDI, a fiber-optic ring network technology. It gives network managers a standard set of variables for monitoring FDDI stations. The RFC has historic status.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1285 lists the variables a network manager can read on FDDI equipment, the fast fibre-optic ring network. The list is copied from the ANSI standard for FDDI with only the wording changed, so any manager's tools can read it.

subtitle: SNMP management objects for FDDI fibre-ring stations, taken from the ANSI station management standard.

tldr.problem: Managers using SNMP needed a standard set of variables for monitoring devices that implement FDDI, and manufacturers wanted to share their instrumentation with other management schemes.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1285 defines the FDDI MIB under { transmission 15 }. It recasts the mandatory variables of the ANSI X3T9.5 station management standard as SNMP objects, grouped into SMT, MAC, PATH, PORT, ATTACHMENT and Chip Sets.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1285 now has Historic status, and the metadata records RFC 1512 as updating it.

facts.label: Object groups
facts.value: 6: SMT, MAC, PATH, PORT, ATTACHMENT, Chip Sets

facts.label: Station identifier
facts.value: 8 octets, low-order 6 from a unique IEEE address

today: RFC 1285 has Historic status, and the metadata records RFC 1512 as updating it. Use the later document as the FDDI MIB definition rather than this one.

sections.title: Purpose and the Network Management Framework
sections.content:
This memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB), the store of managed objects that a network manager reads and writes. It defines objects for managing devices which implement FDDI, the fibre-optic ring network.

The memo sits inside the Internet-standard Network Management Framework, which has three parts. RFC 1155 defines the SMI, the mechanisms used for describing and naming objects for the purpose of management; RFC 1212 gives a more concise description mechanism that is wholly consistent with the SMI. RFC 1156 defines MIB-I, the core set of managed objects for the Internet suite of protocols, and RFC 1213 defines MIB-II, an evolution of MIB-I based on implementation experience and new operational requirements. RFC 1157 defines SNMP, the protocol used for network access to managed objects. The Framework permits new objects to be defined for the purpose of experimentation and evaluation.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a menu of questions you can ask FDDI network equipment, written in the standard menu style that network management tools already use.

sections.title: How Managed Objects Are Named and Coded
sections.content:
Managed objects are reached through a virtual information store, the MIB. Objects are defined using the subset of ASN.1 defined in the SMI. Each object has a name, a syntax and an encoding. The name is an object identifier, an administratively assigned name that specifies an object type, and the object type together with an object instance identifies one specific instantiation of it. For convenience a textual string, called the OBJECT DESCRIPTOR, also names the object type.

The syntax of an object type defines the abstract data structure behind it. ASN.1 is used for this purpose, but the SMI restricts the ASN.1 constructs that may be used, and says these restrictions are made explicitly for simplicity. The encoding is how the object type is represented using that syntax, and it is tied to how the object is transmitted on the network: the SMI specifies the basic encoding rules of ASN.1, subject to the additional requirements imposed by SNMP.

Section 5 holds the specification of every object type in the module, written with the conventions of the SMI as amended by the extensions in RFC 1212.
sections.plainLanguage: Every value has a numbered name, a type, and a way of packing it into bytes for the wire. The memo uses a small, simple subset of ASN.1 so that tools stay easy to write.

sections.title: The ANSI FDDI Standard and This MIB
sections.content:
The module applies to interfaces whose ifType variable in MIB-II has the value fddi(15). For those interfaces, the value of the ifSpecific variable has the object identifier fddi OBJECT IDENTIFIER ::= { transmission 15 }.

The definitions draw heavily on the ANSI X3T9.5 committee and its SMT subcommittee. The memo says the managed objects here are, to the maximum extent possible, identical to those identified by the ANSI committee, so the semantics of each object are the same. Only syntactic changes were made, to recast the objects in terms of the Internet-standard SMI and MIB so that they work with SNMP. The memo gives examples: remapping booleans to enumerated integers and remapping bit strings to octet strings. The naming of the objects was changed as well, for compatibility.

The purpose of those minimal changes with no semantic changes is that implementations of SNMP-manageable FDDI systems can share instrumentation with other network management schemes, which minimises implementation cost and eases the translation of information from one management scheme to another. Only the essential variables were retained, the ones marked mandatory in the ANSI specification, because variables with optional status were perceived as being less widely accepted.
sections.plainLanguage: The questions were copied from the FDDI builders' own rulebook, with only the wording changed so that network management tools can read them.

sections.title: Textual Conventions
sections.content:
The memo introduces several new datatypes as textual conventions. These make the document easier to read and easier to compare with its ANSI counterpart. They change neither the syntax nor the semantics of any managed object, and objects defined in terms of one of them are always encoded by the rules that define the primitive type. The memo is explicit that the conventions are adopted merely for the convenience of readers and writers, so no change to the SMI or to SNMP is needed to accommodate them.

The four conventions are FddiTime, an integer in octet units of 80 nanoseconds used for Path Latency and Synchronous Bandwidth values; FddiResourceId, an integer used to refer to an instance of a MAC, PORT, PATH or ATTACHMENT resource, where indexing begins at 1 and zero means the absence of a resource; FddiSMTStationIdType, an 8-octet identifier for the FDDI station whose low-order six octets come from a unique IEEE-assigned address and whose first two octets are implementor-defined; and FddiMACLongAddressType, a 6-octet MAC address in the IEEE canonical notation.
sections.plainLanguage: A few kinds of answer get their own rules, such as a time, a resource number and a station name. These rules change nothing about the values themselves; they only make the document easier to read.

sections.title: The Groups of Objects and Their Tables
sections.content:
The objects fall into six groups under the fddi node: snmpFddiSMT for station management, snmpFddiMAC, snmpFddiPATH, snmpFddiPORT, snmpFddiATTACHMENT and snmpFddiChipSets. The SMT, MAC, PORT and ATTACHMENT groups are mandatory for all systems which implement manageable FDDI subsystems. The PATH group is empty for now, and shall remain so until the ANSI community sorts out its PATH group. The Chip Set group only allocates object identifiers for PHY and MAC chip sets, and none are defined at present.

Each group has a count object and a table with one row per instance, and most objects carry a REFERENCE to the ANSI object they came from. The SMT group starts with snmpFddiSMTNumber, the number of SMT implementations regardless of their current state. Its table holds the station ID, the operating, highest and lowest SMT version, the counts of MACs, master ports and non-master ports, the configuration capabilities and policies, the connection policy, the neighbour notification timer, and state values such as the ECM and CF states, plus a station action.

The MAC, PORT and ATTACHMENT groups follow the same pattern, holding per-interface objects defined for the corresponding ANSI resources. Some objects are read-only, while others, such as the operating SMT version, the link error rate cutoff and alarm, and the port action, are read-write. The port group reports a link error rate estimate as the absolute value of an exponent, ranging from 10 to the minus 4 to 10 to the minus 15, and describes the connection state as disabled, connecting, standby or active, backed by the more detailed PCM state.
sections.plainLanguage: For each part of the equipment, the manager can ask what it is, what it can do and what it is doing right now. A few settings can also be changed, such as the version in use or the action to run on a port.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo states only that security issues are not discussed in this memo, and it adds no security guidance of its own for the objects it defines.
sections.plainLanguage: The note says nothing about keeping this information safe.

viz.caption: THE OBJECT GROUPS UNDER THE FDDI MIB ROOT

items.label: Out
items.desc: The station is outside the ring.

items.label: In
items.desc: The station is on the ring.

items.label: Leave
items.desc: The station is leaving the ring.

items.label: Path_Test
items.desc: The station is testing its path.

viz.caption: WHAT EACH GROUP OF OBJECTS COVERS

items.title: SMT
items.text: The station as a whole: identity, version, counts, policies and state.

items.title: MAC
items.text: One row per media access control unit in the station.

items.title: PATH
items.text: Left empty until the ANSI community settles its own PATH group.

items.title: PORT
items.text: One row per port: connection state, link error rate and actions.

items.title: ATTACHMENT
items.text: One row per attachment: class, optical bypass and insert policy.

items.title: Chip Sets
items.text: Object identifiers reserved for PHY and MAC chips, none defined yet.
